Enshittification is a pattern where digital platforms progressively degrade the experience for users and business participants as platform owners gain power and begin optimizing for extraction.
It is best understood as a lifecycle, not a one-time event:
1. Early stage: platforms subsidize users with convenience, reach, and low friction to drive rapid adoption.
It is best understood as a lifecycle, not a one-time event:
2. Middle stage: once users are locked in, value shifts toward paying business customers (advertisers, sellers, publishers, developers) to maximize revenue.
It is best understood as a lifecycle, not a one-time event:
3. Late stage: after both sides are dependent, platform owners extract most of the surplus for themselves, reducing quality and fairness for everyone else.
It is best understood as a lifecycle, not a one-time event:
High switching costs and network effects make exit expensive for users and suppliers.
Control over ranking, recommendation, and API access lets platforms change outcomes unilaterally.
Weak Interop and anti-competitive behavior reduce outside alternatives.
Financial pressure and monopoly incentives reward short-term extraction over long-term trust.
Declining relevance/quality in feeds and search.
Increased ads, paywalls, fees, and self-preferencing behavior.
Reduced transparency, portability, and user control.
Policy/rule changes that shift risk and cost onto creators, sellers, or developers.
It provides a practical lens for diagnosing platform decline as a governance and market-structure problem, not just a product-design problem.
It connects personal UX frustration to broader questions of competition policy, rights, and institutional power.
Interoperability requirements and data portability rights.
Competition enforcement against lock-in and self-preferencing.
User and developer leverage through open standards, federation, and exit options.

A heuristic is a useful shortcut: a rule of thumb that usually points the right way but carries no guarantee and can fail when conditions change. An axiom is a statement that can be proven with internal consistency, or an established law of nature—it holds by demonstration, not by convenience.

The distinction matters because the two are easily confused. A heuristic that held reliably in one era gets repeated until it is treated as a law, long after the conditions that made it true have passed.

Treating a heuristic as an axiom hides its assumptions. When those assumptions lapse, the "law" keeps getting cited with the same confidence, and the error compounds because no one re-examines a premise they believe is proven.
The garden tracks the two families separately: defeasible, named generalizations are Logseq/Entity/Named Law instances; genuinely provable or physical statements are Logseq/Entity/Axiom instances.

An EPUB file is a ZIP archive with the .epub extension, containing a fixed internal directory layout rather than an arbitrary set of files.
mimetype — the first entry in the archive, stored uncompressed, containing exactly the ASCII string application/epub+zip.
META-INF/container.xml — points a reading system at the location of the package document inside the archive.

the package document (e.g. EPUB/package.opf) — an XML file with three parts: metadata (title, author, identifier, in Dublin Core), manifest (every file in the archive, with an id and media type), and spine (the linear reading order, referencing manifest items).
content documents — XHTML files, one per chapter or section, referenced from the spine.
a navigation document (nav.xhtml) — an XHTML file with a nav element that serves as the table of contents; EPUB 2 used a separate toc.ncx file for the same purpose.
supporting resources — CSS stylesheets, images, and embedded fonts, stored alongside the content documents.

EPUB is a W3C Recommendation. It was originally developed by the International Digital Publishing Forum (IDPF), which merged into the W3C in 2017; the W3C has published the specification since EPUB 3.2.
The package document builds on the Open Packaging Format (OPF) and Dublin Core metadata; content documents are XHTML.
Native or first-party support: Apple Books (macOS, iOS), Google Play Books (Android, web).
Cross-platform readers and converters: calibre, Adobe Digital Editions.
E-ink devices: Kobo readers support EPUB natively; Amazon Kindle devices do not read EPUB directly and require conversion.
EPUB 2 (2007) — the OPF/OCF-based container with an NCX-based table of contents.
EPUB 3.0 (2011) — added XHTML5 content documents, embedded fonts, and Media Overlays (synchronized audio).
EPUB 3.2 (2019) — first version published directly by the W3C after the IDPF merger.
EPUB 3.3 (2023) — current W3C Recommendation, consolidating the EPUB 3 family of specifications.

Short answer: no clear consensus, but the leading theories point to high-flown/high-flying, not to playing high notes on a flute.
First attested as U.S. slang in 1839 (as a noun by 1848), from folk speech rather than any single documented coinage. (Etymonline)
High-flown / high-flying — Etymonline's lead guess, and the theory Random House's historical dictionary also favors as most probable. (Etymonline, Grammarphobia)

Fluting — American Heritage Dictionary suggests "high" + "fluting," i.e. someone who thinks too highly of himself is "high-fluting." Merriam-Webster hedges the same way. This is the closest match to the guess above, but even the dictionaries proposing it call it uncertain, and one critic (Grammarphobia) notes it cuts against the etymology since flutes were originally humble farmers' instruments, not symbols of pretension.

Steamboat smokestacks — a folk theory (via broadcaster Melvyn Bragg) that wealthy 1800s riverboat passengers were called "highfalutin'" because of the "high fluted smokestacks" that carried soot away from them. If "fluting" is the root at all, this architectural/grooved sense (like fluted columns) is the more plausible link, not the musical sense of playing high notes.
Yiddish — a proposed derivation from "hifelufelem" ("nonsense"), floated as plausible by sound alone but not well evidenced.

On the specific guess: "fluting" here, in every version of the theory, means grooved/pipe-shaped (as in a fluted column or a fluted smokestack) or the instrument itself as a symbol, not the act of playing high notes. And it's only one of several competing, unproven theories, not the accepted origin.

Old English bana meant "killer, slayer, murderer, a worker of death", whether a person, an animal or a thing. It descends from Proto-Germanic *banon, and is cognate with Old Norse bani ("death") and Gothic banja ("stroke, wound"). (Etymonline)
Where does the phrase "the bane of my existence" come from?
Poison sense — "bane" also came to mean deadly poison, which survives in plant names like wolfsbane and henbane. (Wiktionary, Today I Found Out)
Where does the phrase "the bane of my existence" come from?
Softening to "ruin" — by the 1570s "bane" meant "that which causes woe or ruin", no longer requiring a death. (Etymonline)
Where does the phrase "the bane of my existence" come from?

"Of my existence" — an intensifier that makes the annoyance the ruin of one's whole life, said with humor. Saying "the bane of my existence" about a printer is a mock-tragic use of a word that once named a murderer.
